definition: Lurid means ghastly and sensational — horror played up for shock.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word lurid. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know lurid should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The documentary skips lurid reenactments entirely and lets the court transcripts speak.
Vivid is bright and lifelike but honest — it stops well short of lurid, which cranks the horror for effect.
Ghoulish goes further than lurid: past shock for the audience into open relish of the gruesome itself.

Sensational means pumped up to thrill or shock — the tabloid tone any exciting story can take on. Lurid is darker and more specific: sensationalism about the ghastly, horror cranked up for effect. A celebrity scandal can be sensational without being lurid; lurid needs gore or dread in the telling.

Gruesome describes the content itself — genuinely horrifying material that needs no exaggeration, like a crash scene or a battlefield. Lurid instead accuses the presentation: the same material dressed up to shock. A plain report of a disaster is gruesome; a retelling in blood-soaked headlines has turned lurid.
held deliberately back
plain reporting, no drama at all

Latin luror, the sickly-yellow word behind lurid, produced no other common English descendant — the root's entire legacy is this one adjective, which drifted from death-pale color to the glare of sensational detail.

The museum's plague exhibit drew complaints for its lurid wall panels — boils rendered in wet reds, a looping soundtrack of moans — while the curators' own catalog told the same history in careful, quiet prose.
Lurid is exact because the fault lies in the telling, not the facts: the panels crank horror up for effect.
The same history told plainly is merely grim; dressed in dripping red and staged shrieks, it turns lurid.
Lurid condemns how a thing is told or shown: details chosen to shock, horror played for thrills.
Gruesome describes the content itself; lurid accuses the presentation.

When the old mill burned down, the town's two news outlets covered the same fire.
The Gazette reported the cause, the damage, and the single injury in three careful paragraphs.
The Nightly Wire went lurid instead: its post opened on 'flesh-searing flames,' lingered over the injured watchman's burns, and scored the video with screams pulled from a stock library.
Readers noticed that nothing in the Wire's version added a single fact.
The paper had simply dressed a small fire in gore and dread, because dread is what sells.
